sections.title: Context
sections.body: Telefonica Alpha, in collaboration with Harvard Medical School. Applying behaviour change science to health product journey design.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: Health services were improving usability without improving outcomes. A smoother screen flow does not change whether someone takes their medication, attends their appointment, or follows through on a health programme. The business problem was that products were being measured on engagement metrics that didn't track to clinical outcomes — and investment was going into UX improvements that made little difference at the health outcome level.

sections.title: My role
sections.body: I led the design work: running workshops with Harvard Medical School researchers to translate behaviour change principles into practical journey design, then working with product and engineering teams to implement these at specific touchpoints. The theoretical framework was provided by Harvard; the translation into product decisions was mine.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: The framework drew on Kahneman's research on cognitive biases and BJ Fogg's Behaviour Model (behaviour = motivation + ability + prompt). The insight is that behaviour change happens when the environment makes the desired behaviour easy, timely, and rewarding — not through information or willpower. I designed the journey to identify moments of high motivation (after a health scare, at the start of a new treatment, following a positive result) and meet users at those moments with low-friction actions. Specific techniques embedded included commitment devices at enrolment, progress visualisation, social norms at drop-off risk points, and individually calibrated reminders rather than fixed schedules.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: The journey design framework was adopted as a standard approach for health product design at Telefonica Alpha and subsequently at Koa Health. It directly influenced the design of the Perspectives programme structure and the engagement approach in Fluid, where the time-mood connection was designed as a behaviour change tool rather than a tracking feature.
